citation: Lombard, Matthew, and Theresa Ditton. "At the Heart of It All: The Concept of Presence." Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication 3, no. 2 (1997): JCMC321. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1083-6101.1997.tb00072.x
thesis: Presence -- the perceptual illusion that a mediated experience is not mediated -- is practically and theoretically important but remains fragmentary and unsystematic as a research object because scholars across communication, psychology, computer science, engineering, philosophy, and the arts approach it from separate literatures with no shared operational core; this article synthesizes six distinct conceptualizations (social richness, realism, transportation, immersion, social actor within medium, medium as social actor) into a single unifying definition -- the perceptual illusion of nonmediation, occurring via an invisible-medium or a transformed-medium mechanism -- surveys existing evidence and speculation about presence's causes (form, content, and user-characteristic variables) and effects (physiological and psychological), and recommends the attributes of a systematic future research program.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Catalogues mid-1990s presence-producing technologies (VR, simulation rides, IMAX, videoconferencing, talking computers); states practical (design/profitability) and theoretical (mediated-stimuli-as-substitute-for-nonmediated-stimuli assumption) rationale for studying presence; previews the article's three-part task.

sections.title: Concept Explication -- six conceptualizations of presence
sections.summary: Reviews presence as (1) social richness (social presence theory, media richness theory), (2) realism (social realism vs. perceptual realism), (3) transportation ('you are there' / 'it is here' / 'we are together'), (4) immersion (perceptual + psychological), (5) social actor within medium (parasocial interaction, Horton & Wohl 1956), (6) medium as social actor (Reeves & Nass's CASA program).

sections.title: Presence Explicated -- the unifying definition
sections.summary: Synthesizes the six conceptualizations into a formal definition: presence is the perceptual illusion of nonmediation, occurring via an invisible/transparent-medium mechanism or a transformed-into-social-entity mechanism; presence is framed as a property of the person, occurring in discrete instants rather than continuous degree, resulting from an interaction of media-form, media-content, and media-user characteristics.

sections.title: Causes of Presence as Invisible Medium
sections.summary: Surveys form variables (sensory-output breadth/depth; visual-display characteristics -- image quality, size, viewing distance/field of view, motion, color, dimensionality, camera technique; aural characteristics -- quality, dimensionality; stimuli for other senses -- olfactory, body movement, tactile, force feedback; interactivity; obtrusiveness; live vs. recorded/constructed status; number of people), content variables (social realism, use of media conventions, nature of task/activity), and media-user variables (willingness to suspend disbelief, knowledge/prior experience with the medium, other user traits).

sections.title: Causes of Presence as Transformed Medium
sections.summary: Parallel, shorter causal survey for the transformed-medium mechanism: form variables (interactivity, use of voice, medium size/shape), content variables (social realism, use of media conventions, nature of task/activity), media-user variables (knowledge/prior experience, age, gender, personality).

sections.title: Effects of Presence
sections.summary: Physiological effects of presence as invisible medium (arousal; vection and simulation sickness -- dizziness, eyestrain, disorientation, dysphoria, nausea; other physiological changes such as reduced eye-hand coordination); psychological effects of presence as invisible medium (enjoyment, involvement, task performance, skills training, desensitization, persuasion, memory and social judgment/source-monitoring errors, parasocial interaction); psychological effects of presence as transformed medium (perceived computer 'personality,' gender-stereotyped responses to computers).

sections.title: Future Presence Research
sections.summary: Calls for standardized conceptual and operational definitions; a combined subjective (questionnaire) and objective (physiological/behavioral) measurement instrument; standardized manipulation of causal variables (illustrated via a cautionary example of inconsistent image-size labeling across prior studies). Closes with open, deliberately unresolved questions: is presence necessarily good; can its intensity be user-controlled; can it contribute to dissociative/psychotic symptoms; is the desire for presence rooted in evolved threat-detection; will presence-rich mediated interaction with real people break down or extend social stereotypes.

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: core object of the article; source's own 'you are there'/'it is here' transportation subtypes are the clearest spatial-presence instances -- user transported to a mediated place, or objects/people transported into the user's environment

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: source's own 'presence as social richness' (social presence theory, media richness theory) plus the 'we are together' shared-space transportation subtype

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: source's own 'presence as immersion': perceptual component (objective sensory submersion via HMD/headphones/gloves) plus psychological component (involvement, absorption, engrossment)

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: primary causal variable for both mechanisms of presence; five subsidiary dimensions -- number of inputs accepted, number/type of modifiable characteristics, range of possible change, input-response correspondence, response speed

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: source's own 'presence as realism', split into perceptual realism (objects/people look/sound/feel real) and social realism (plausible, 'true to life' content)

constructs.label: cybersickness & physical discomfort
constructs.treatment: 'vection and simulation sickness' -- physiological effect of presence combined with illusion of self-motion: dizziness, eyestrain, disorientation, dysphoria, nausea

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: 'enjoyment' named as presence's most prominent psychological impact, linked to commercial popularity of presence-evoking technologies; article notes little direct research testing the link at time of writing

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: 'involvement' effect (fun, exciting, competitive, addictive, intense); Heeter's (1995) BattleTech VR survey factor-analysis reported as highest-rated factor (8.7/10) among several

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: 'skills training' effect domain; flight-simulator and ARI virtual-navigation-training studies cited as evidence high-presence media improve trained performance over low-presence alternatives, with explicit caveats about transfer risk

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: 'memory and social judgment' effect domain; presence-enhancing viewing conditions linked (Ditton 1997) to greater source-monitoring error -- misattribution of fictional mediated information to real-world social judgments

readings.claim: Presence is formally defined as 'the perceptual illusion of nonmediation': a person's failure to perceive or acknowledge the existence of a medium, responding as though the medium were not there.
This illusion occurs via one of two mechanisms: the medium becomes perceptually invisible/transparent (an 'open window'), or the medium is perceptually transformed into an independent social entity.

Presence is a property of the person, not the medium, though resulting from an interaction of media-form, media-content, and media-user characteristics; it occurs in discrete instants rather than continuous degree.

All six conceptualizations of presence found across the literature (social richness, realism, transportation, immersion, social actor within medium, medium as social actor) are subsumed by the unifying definition, each representing one or more aspects of the perceptual illusion of nonmediation.
Causes of presence divide into form, content, and user-characteristic variables, applied separately to the invisible-medium and transformed-medium mechanisms, yielding a six-cell causal framework.

Effects of presence are physiological (arousal; vection/simulation sickness; reflexive responses; transient after-effects) and psychological (enjoyment, involvement, task performance, skills-training benefit, desensitization, persuasion, memory/source-monitoring effects, intensified parasocial interaction).

Systematic presence research requires standardized conceptual/operational definitions, a combined subjective-and-objective measurement instrument, and standardized manipulation of causal variables; prior image-size studies are cited as a cautionary example of incomparable, inconsistently labeled manipulations.

The article closes with deliberately unresolved questions: whether presence is necessarily desirable, whether its intensity should be user-controllable, whether it can contribute to dissociative/psychotic symptoms, whether the desire for presence has an evolutionary threat-detection basis, and whether presence-rich mediated interaction will erode or reinforce social stereotypes.

interlocutors.name: Biocca, Frank
interlocutors.role: source of perceptual/psychological immersion definitions (with Delaney/Levy) and interactivity input-channel taxonomy

interlocutors.name: Steuer, Jonathan
interlocutors.role: source of the vividness (sensory breadth/depth) and interactivity (temporal ordering, spatial organization, mapping) frameworks underlying the causes-of-presence sections

interlocutors.name: Heeter, Carrie
interlocutors.role: source of the range/intensity-of-stimuli definition of presence and the BattleTech VR involvement-survey data

interlocutors.name: Held, Richard & Durlach, Nathaniel
interlocutors.role: cited for the observation that no scientific body of theory/data underlay presence's causes at time of writing, and for the recommended subjective+objective measurement design

interlocutors.name: Short, Williams & Christie
interlocutors.role: source of social presence theory, the sociability/warmth/intimacy conceptualization measured via semantic-differential items

interlocutors.name: Reeves, Byron & Nass, Clifford
interlocutors.role: source of the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) research program; source of the closing evolutionary-threat-detection speculation

interlocutors.name: Horton, Donald & Wohl, R. Richard
interlocutors.role: source of the 1956 'parasocial interaction' terminology underlying presence as social actor within medium

interlocutors.name: Slater, Mel & Usoh, Martin
interlocutors.role: source of the 'you are there' virtual-presence definition (suspension of disbelief re: being in a world other than one's real location)

interlocutors.name: Ditton, Theresa (self-citation)
interlocutors.role: co-author's own 1997 study cited as tentative empirical support for mediated/nonmediated memory confusion, and as the screen-size/source-monitoring-error study

interlocutors.name: Muhlbach, Bocker & Prussog
interlocutors.role: source of the 'telepresence in video communications' operational definition and videoconferencing shared-space measures

interlocutors.name: Sheridan, Thomas
interlocutors.role: source of the teleoperation/telepresence vs. virtual-presence distinction and the open question of whether presence is benign or a distraction from task performance

tensions.axis: presence as invisible medium vs. presence as transformed medium
tensions.note: The article's own dual-mechanism framework is presented as parallel and non-competing, not adjudicated between; both mechanisms receive full form/content/user causal treatments (FE).

tensions.axis: presence as technology-determined (form/immersion-driven) vs. presence as psychologically/individually-determined (user variables: willingness to suspend disbelief, prior experience, personality)
tensions.note: (P/anticipatory-application) Lombard & Ditton's own two-track causal framework instantiates this cluster's debate axis #3 (plan §3 seed 3) before Witmer & Singer or Chow formalize either pole explicitly; the source itself does not adjudicate between the tracks, treating both as necessary jointly.

tensions.axis: presence as unconditional good (enjoyment, learning benefit) vs. presence as risk (desensitization, source-monitoring memory errors, possible link to dissociative symptoms)
tensions.note: The article's own closing section raises this ambivalence explicitly as an open question rather than resolving it (FE).
